structure.title: The defence · A reputation enters court
structure.text: Before Socrates answers the formal charges, he tackles an older picture of himself circulating among the jurors. His account of questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen explains both his occupation and why so many people have reason to dislike him.

structure.title: The penalty · Name your price
structure.text: A new procedural question forces Socrates to say what treatment his life deserves. Any proposal he makes will reveal how far he is willing to accept the court's account of the service he has rendered Athens.

structure.title: Final words · Two audiences
structure.text: Socrates speaks differently to the citizens who voted against him and those who favoured him. Death, which could serve simply as the most powerful argument for pleading, becomes one more subject about which somebody might claim to know too much.

people.name: Socrates
people.text: He tells the jury he will speak plainly, without the tearful appeals they expect. His defence becomes an account of how he has spent his life, questioning anyone with a reputation for wisdom, and why he will not stop.

people.name: Meletus
people.role: An accuser called upon to answer
people.text: The prosecution has accused Socrates of corrupting the young. In their short exchange Socrates asks who actually improves them, turning an accusation about one man's influence into a much larger claim about education.

people.name: Chaerephon
people.text: His question to the oracle leaves Socrates with a puzzle about wisdom. The resulting investigation depends on the difference between being skilled at something and being able to say where that skill ends.

context.title: The title means a defence
context.text: Plato gives us a speech addressed to citizen jurors. Its speaker has to decide, repeatedly, whether the means most likely to save him would contradict the life he is trying to justify.

notice.text: Listen for requests about speaking style.
notice.why: Socrates asks the jury to tolerate the sound of ordinary conversation. The request already puts something on trial alongside his conduct, namely the court's idea of how a truthful man ought to sound.

passages.quote: so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth.

notice.text: Count the occasions on which fear could settle an argument.
notice.why: Military service, political orders and the prospect of death supply different pressures to give way. Socrates brings them together to establish what sort of evidence fear could possibly offer about what is right.

opening: Socrates is on trial for his life, and a more accommodating defendant might apologise. Instead, he explains why Athens needs someone who keeps embarrassing its most confident citizens. He has spent years asking people to account for what they claim to know; now the city has the power to make him stop. Plato's account of his defence turns a courtroom into a final public demonstration of the habit under prosecution, with a verdict that matters considerably more than winning an argument.
